Introduction: What “spatial poverty” means at a core level
- Core concept: Spatial poverty treats poverty as inherently a geographic phenomenon whose incidence, persistence, and severity vary across space, and whose meanings and thresholds are shaped by place, time, and institutions. <cite id="f215da46-0">In this view, poverty is not fixed in content but “changes significantly due to the influence of spatial dimensions,” so that “the content of the concept of poverty changes significantly due to the influence of spatial dimensions.”</cite> <cite id="f215da46-1">A spatial poverty theory maintains that “geographical location plays an important role in the formation and persistence of poverty” and has given rise to related ideas such as spatial poverty traps that can be empirically tested.</cite>
- Lineage and framing: <cite id="f215da46-1">Although environmental determinism has fallen out of favor, the “spatiality of poverty” has grown in relevance; spatial poverty theory inherits from determinism but emphasizes location’s role interacting with human decisions and institutions.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-0">Geographical approaches clarify the spatial distribution of poverty and emphasize how physical environment, infrastructure, distance to public resources, and demographic characteristics determine or interact with poverty in a place; possibilistic perspectives argue institutions and governance failures create spatial poverty traps.</cite>

Conceptual foundations and typologies
- Poverty as relative and multidimensional: <cite id="f215da46-2">There is no universally accepted, objective definition of poverty; institutions use different dimensions (income/expenditure, capabilities, social inclusion), reflecting multidimensional deprivation and context dependence.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-4">Poverty can be framed as income shortfalls, basic needs unmet, or capability deprivation, and is multidimensional, encompassing lack of access to health and education, social isolation, and powerlessness.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-2">The capability perspective defines poverty as deprivation of basic capabilities (nutrition, clothing, shelter, participation), not just low income.</cite>
- Absolute vs. relative poverty: <cite id="852e0cef-2">An absolute poverty line is the minimum income or consumption needed to meet basic needs (e.g., food, clothing, shelter), a concept rooted in work such as Ravallion (1992).</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-2">Relative poverty adjusts to average or median consumption levels; it classifies who is poor and tracks differences across regions by comparing households to local norms.</cite> <cite id="1c02d7de-1">Poverty is neither strictly absolute nor relative; definitions carry elements of both and are contested across the literature.</cite>
- Spatial poverty as a multidimensional/spatial deprivation concept: <cite id="1c02d7de-2">The World Bank’s early articulation of “multidimensional relative poverty” emphasized that human poverty encompasses lack of income and objective deprivations such as drinking water, roads, sanitation, and subjective perceptions of deprivation; later work expanded to spatial and ethnic-area analyses.</cite> <cite id="1c02d7de-0">Multidimensional relative poverty is a dynamic form in which health, education, and living standards fall significantly below the socially recognized average due to uneven development and endowment disparities, with EU-style thresholds like 60% of median income used for relative poverty measurement.</cite>

How “spatial poverty” is defined and operationalized in practice
- Income-based spatial thresholds and classification:
  - Global and national poverty lines: <cite id="852e0cef-0">The World Bank’s international poverty line is $1.90 per person per day (2011 PPPs), with lower- and upper-middle-income thresholds around $3.20 and $5.50 per day, used to classify households as poor based on income shortfalls.</cite>
  - Place-based relative thresholds: <cite id="852e0cef-1">Policy maps often classify “high-poverty tracts” using federal thresholds such as areas with >40% of the population below the official poverty line, or >20% for “extreme poverty” tracts; alternative lower thresholds (e.g., >30%) are used to capture concentrated poverty differently across metros.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-1">Relative, regional thresholds using 50% of local median income reveal a much greater extent and different geographic distribution of concentrated poverty than the federal line, underscoring how definition choice changes spatial patterns.</cite> <cite id="1c02d7de-0">EU practice uses 60% of median disposable income as a relative poverty threshold, with similar regional variants used elsewhere (50–40% of average or income) to reflect local standards.</cite>
  - Household targeting: <cite id="852e0cef-2">Once a line is set, incidence, depth, and severity are quantified using the Foster–Greer–Thorbecke (FGT) indices; headcount, gap, and squared gap measures formalize who is poor and how deprived they are.</cite>
- HDI-based spatial deprivation and multidimensional mapping:
  - Composite welfare benchmarks: <cite id="f215da46-1">Human Development Index (HDI) aggregates life expectancy, education, and income to capture welfare levels across countries and regions, providing a multidimensional reference for identifying spatial deprivation in rich and poor places.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-2">UNHDR defines poverty as “inadequacy of resources and deprivation of choices that would enable people to enjoy decent living conditions,” aligning with HDI-style multidimensional poverty concepts.</cite>
  - Operationalization in mapping: <cite id="852e0cef-0">Geographical theory is used to delineate spatial poverty by identifying areas where physical-environmental constraints, infrastructure deficits, distance to services, and governance failures co-locate to produce deprivation relative to regional standards.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-3">Administrative and empirical practice show that poverty is widely dispersed with localized concentrations; regional clustering and “spatial concentration effects” are often due to industry agglomeration and scale effects, motivating fine-scale (village-level) mapping for policy design.</cite>
- Spatial clustering and spillovers:
  - Concentration and outliers: <cite id="852e0cef-1">High-poverty “tracts” are commonly defined by thresholds like >40% under the line; studies vary thresholds (20–30–40%) to capture concentration versus isolated pockets.</cite>
  - Statistical diagnostics: <cite id="852e0cef-1">Relative definitions (e.g., 50% of median) reveal different spatial patterns and more widespread concentrated poverty than the federal line, highlighting sensitivity to the definition of “poverty” and its spatial distribution.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-4">Spatial clustering is assessed with local Moran’s I: counties with significantly positive neighbor correlations at standardized values >2 are “concentrations,” those with <−2 are “outliers,” enabling categorization of spatial outliers and clustered hotspots alongside poverty intensity.</cite>
- Country-level examples and measurement integration:
  - China’s rural line and MPI: <cite id="852e0cef-3">China’s rural poverty line tracked near the World Bank international threshold (2300–3535 yuan; ~$1.80–$2.76/day), enabling spatial targeting; multidimensional poverty indices (MPI) complement income lines, though indicator selection is challenging and single-dimensional measures remain common due to data simplicity.</cite>
  - Environmental–institutional determinants: <cite id="852e0cef-0">Geography-based poverty mapping integrates physical environment, infrastructure, distance to services, and governance quality to explain spatially varying poverty patterns and the risk of spatial poverty traps.</cite>

Mechanisms, evolution, and spatial spillovers
- Causal mechanisms: <cite id="852e0cef-0">Spatial poverty arises from interactions between physical conditions (vegetation, climate, soils, disasters, land use, resources) and human decisions, with infrastructure access, distance to public resources, and demographics shaping local deprivation; institutional and political failures produce spatial poverty traps.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-1">Geography of poverty explains the distribution, types, and evolutionary mechanisms of poverty, including interactions with the physical environment and anti-poverty interventions.</cite>
- Concentration, diffusion, and scale effects: <cite id="852e0cef-3">Globally, poverty areas tend to fragment spatially rather than expand in mass; at regional scales, poor areas cluster due to industry agglomeration, exhibiting spatial scale effects that matter for policy design.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-4">Local Moran’s I identifies spatial “concentrations” and “outliers,” revealing how poverty coevolves with wealth in contiguous counties and how isolated pockets reflect cross-border disparities.</cite>
- Measurement integration with welfare indicators: <cite id="852e0cef-2">FGT indices quantify incidence, depth, and severity of poverty once a threshold is chosen; inflation adjustment and adult-equivalence scaling are used to compare household status over time and space.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-1">The shift from one-dimensional lines to multidimensional indices reflects mainstreaming of poverty’s spatial and multidimensional qualities in theory and measurement.</cite>

Choice of definitions, scale, and critiques
- Relativity, arbitrariness, and context: <cite id="f215da46-4">There is no objectively correct poverty definition; different concepts and measures yield very different poverty rates and profiles, so clearer definitions suited to political, economic, and social context are essential.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-2">Definitions range from income shortfalls to basic needs to capability deprivation; each embeds different reference standards and may capture different aspects of deprivation.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-2">Absolute lines (minimum needs baskets) vs. relative lines (local averages/medians) imply different spatial classifications and target sets, with relative measures capturing inequality and place-based deprivation more directly.</cite>
- Threshold design and scale sensitivity: <cite id="852e0cef-1">Federal 40% thresholds and 50% of median income alternatives produce different spatial maps and concentration metrics, showing how threshold choice shapes conclusions about spatial poverty.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-1">Using a single monetary norm (e.g., 40% standard) can become “divorced from the realities of our affluent society,” motivating relative-region definitions that better capture meaningful differences across places.</cite>
- Data, indicators, and integration: <cite id="852e0cef-3">Multidimensional poverty measurement (MPI) integrates deprivations across health, education, and living standards, but indicator selection and data availability complicate implementation; single-dimensional lines remain common due to ease of use.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-3">Remote sensing (nighttime lights), internet/social media, and mobile phone transaction footprints enable proxy estimation of spatial poverty, complementing surveys and administrative data.</cite>
- Spatial methodology cautions: <cite id="852e0cef-0">Geographical poverty research clarifies local determinants and mechanisms, but thresholds and classifications hinge on context-specific standards; misaligning thresholds to place or time (e.g., fixed absolute baskets across regions) can distort spatial identification.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-2">Headcount and gap measures are sensitive to the poverty line; severity weights amplify inequality among the poor, so line choice and equivalence scales materially affect spatial poverty estimates.</cite>

Practical implications for defining and mapping spatial poverty
- Policy-relevant definitions:
  - Absolute-income poverty for targeting extreme deprivation (global lines; local baskets) to prioritize survival needs. <cite id="852e0cef-0">Global and national lines (e.g., $1.90/day) identify households below minimum needs and guide emergency and extreme poverty interventions.</cite>
  - Relative-income thresholds (e.g., 40–50% or 60% of median) to capture place-based deprivation and concentrated poverty for spatial planning. <cite id="852e0cef-1">Threats like >20–40% poverty delineate neighborhood-scale need; 50% of median income reveals broader concentrated poverty than official lines.</cite>
  - HDI/MPI-based spatial deprivation for multidimensional needs (health, education, infrastructure), recognizing capability loss and social exclusion. <cite id="1c02d7de-2">Multidimensional relative poverty integrates income and deprivations such as water, roads, sanitation, and subjective deprivation to reflect local living standards.</cite>
- Methods to implement:
  - Set a threshold; compute headcount and FGT indices; map spatial units using tract/county boundaries; test clustering with Moran’s I; classify concentrations/outliers; and create decile/ranking profiles combining intensity and spatial pattern. <cite id="852e0cef-2">Headcount, gap, and severity provide intensity metrics once the line is chosen.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-4">Local Moran’s I with standardized cutoffs (>2 or <−2 at p<0.05) identifies clustered hotspots and spatial outliers for spatial narratives.</cite>
- Governance and context: <cite id="852e0cef-0">Institutional and political factors can embed spatial poverty traps; mapping should integrate infrastructure access, distance to services, and governance quality to target structural bottlenecks alongside household income shortfalls.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-4">Because poverty is multidimensional, relying solely on income understates deprivation; integrating access, social inclusion, and power differentials yields a more actionable definition for place-based policy.</cite>

Summary answer to “What is spatial poverty and how is it defined?”
- Definition: Spatial poverty is the condition in which households or communities experience deprivation relative to locally recognized standards of living and access to goods and services, with incidence, intensity, and persistence varying across geographic space; poverty’s content is relational and contextual, shifting with place, time, and institutions. <cite id="f215da46-0">The concept of poverty changes significantly due to spatial dimensions.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-1">Geographical location plays an important role in the formation and persistence of poverty.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-0">Geographical theory explains spatial distribution and mechanisms, including interactions with physical environment and governance failures that produce spatial poverty traps.</cite>
- Core conceptual axes: It is neither purely absolute nor purely relative; it is multidimensional and dynamic across space and time, integrating income shortfalls with non-monetary deprivations and spillovers. <cite id="852e0cef-2">Absolute poverty lines fix minimum needs baskets; relative lines adjust to local averages/medians; both have roles but are context-dependent.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-3">Spatial poverty often combines widespread dispersion with localized concentrations shaped by regional industry and scale effects.</cite>
- Operational definitions used:
  - Income-based poverty lines (global $1.90/day; national/local thresholds) to classify households below minimum needs and compute FGT measures of incidence, depth, and severity. <cite id="852e0cef-0">World Bank international poverty line ($1.90/day) and national thresholds (e.g., China’s 2300–3535 yuan) classify who is poor.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-2">FGT indices quantify poverty once a threshold is set.</cite>
  - Relative thresholds tied to local medians (e.g., 40–50–60% of median income) to identify concentrated poverty and spatial outliers. <cite id="852e0cef-1">Federal 40%/20% tract thresholds and 50% of median income alternatives reveal different spatial extents and clustering.</cite> <cite id="1c02d7de-0">EU uses 60% of median income as a relative poverty threshold; 50–40% variants are used elsewhere.</cite>
  - Multidimensional spatial deprivation using HDI/MPI and related indices, integrating health, education, infrastructure, and subjective deprivation; often complemented by remote-sensing proxies. <cite id="1c02d7de-2">The World Bank’s multidimensional relative poverty links income with deprivations such as water, roads, sanitation, and perceptions.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-3">MPI and alternative composite indicators provide comprehensive views, supported by nightlights and digital footprints for proxy estimation.</cite>
  - Spatial pattern diagnostics (e.g., local Moran’s I) to classify “concentrated” vs. “outlier” areas and combine intensity with spatial configuration for targeting and narrative. <cite id="852e0cef-4">Local Moran’s I with standardized cutoffs identifies significant clustering and outliers, enabling 10-category county typologies that combine rate and pattern.</cite>
- Caveats: Thresholds and definitions are political and empirical choices; small changes in reference standards (absolute vs. relative, basket content, equivalence scales, spatial resolution) produce large changes in who is classified as poor and where. <cite id="f215da46-4">Different concepts and measures yield very different poverty rates and profiles; there is no objectively correct definition.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-1">Federal 40% standards can understate disparities; using 50% of median income changes spatial conclusions.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-2">Indicator selection and basket equivalence affect estimates; severity weights emphasize inequality among the poor, underscoring the need for transparent, context-appropriate definitions.</cite>

Snippet: At the fundamental level is the question of who qualifies as the poor or what is poverty. This conceptual question has plagued development practices and policymakers for several decades. The task of defining poverty assumed greater relevance in the 1960s in the aftermath of the attainment of political independence by many former colonies (Lee & Braithwaite, 2022). Suffice it to state that defining poverty or even the approach to doing this, is a strongly contested issue and the different positions are not always necessarily complementary. One of the well-known theorizations in this endeavour is the capability approach by Sen (1982Sen ( , 2000) ) who posits that the specification of a certain consumption norm or of a poverty line does only a part of the job. This notwithstanding, the World Bank still annually publishes its report based on a hypothetical dollar per person per day metriccurrently, 1.9 USD per person per day -as the so-called poverty line while the United Nations produces its annual reports on the human development index -a composite of life expectancy, education and standard of living -to measure welfare levels in individual countries. There has been a clear move towards indices as the multidimensional nature of poverty has become more mainstream (Alkire & Foster, 2011). 

A key development in this theoretical evolution has been the discovery of the spatial qualities of poverty and deprivation. The theory of spatial poverty can be traced back to the theory of environmental determinism -the idea that the physical environment predisposes regions and countries to particular development trajectories. While environmental determinism has largely been rejected in favour of environmental possibilism, the spatiality of poverty continues to grow in relevance (Bird et al., 2010;Burke & Jayne, 2008;Elwood et al., 2016). Like its antecedent, the spatial poverty theory holds that geographical location plays an important role in the formation and persistence of poverty (Zhou & Liu, 2022). Snippet: Reducing poverty and inequality is a cornerstone of development policy of any nation [1]. Poverty definitions and measurements have important ramifications for targeting its reduction strategies [2]. While there is a widespread agreement on the desirability of poverty reduction, defining poverty is more controversial. On the other hand, some scholars have attempted a broader definition of what constitutes poverty than simply relying on the federal definition, which is derived from the cost of a minimum acceptable diet of food, albeit using a multiplier that reflects food expenditures as a percentage of income in the mid-1960s, rather than the present day. Swanstrom, Ryan, and Stigers (2008) have argued that "[the 40%] standard. . .has become increasingly divorced from the realities of our affluent society and ignores differences across metropolitan areas" and have instead opted to use "a relative definition of poverty based on 50 percent of median income in each region. . .find [ing] that the extent, geographic distribution, and trends in concentrated poverty between 1990 and 2000 are very different from those found using the federal poverty standard" (p. 295). That is, due to the inflexibility in the definition of the federal poverty line in the first place, current indicators, whether using a 40% threshold or something lower, fail to capture the meaningful differences between places and the unequal distribution of poverty between them. Using this expanded definition based on median household income, Swanstrom et al. (2008) not only show the extent of concentrated poverty to be much greater than is assumed under conventional definitions, but also that places that might otherwise not be classified as high-poverty areas are actually considerably more disadvantaged than some places that would be under conventional definitions.

Snippet: Current research on multidimensional relative poverty focuses on three key areas. First, the conceptual evolution of multidimensional relative poverty. Poverty studies have gradually shifted from absolute and relative poverty to multidimensional and multidimensional relative poverty. Initially, absolute poverty was defined as a state where a household's total income could not cover the basic necessities required by all its members to maintain normal bodily functions (6). With a deeper understanding of poverty, scholars argued that it also includes relative exclusion and deprivation, leading to the development of the relative poverty theory (7). However, relative poverty has its limitations (8), necessitating consideration of various factors that affect the long-term wellbeing of impoverished individuals, such as health, education, and quality of life (9). Consequently, some scholars argue for the establishment of a multidimensional poverty measurement system to address the comprehensive development needs of the poor (10). While multidimensional relative poverty is distinct from multidimensional poverty, the concept of relative poverty emphasizes differences among individuals. Its measurement dimensions and indicators cannot be directly equated with those of multidimensional poverty. Furthermore, existing research on multidimensional relative poverty often adopts the measurement dimensions of multidimensional poverty without adequately addressing the distinctions in measurement elements (11). Multidimensional relative poverty is a dynamic form of poverty characterized by a state of living in which a family's health, education, and standard of living are significantly below the socially recognized average due to factors such as uneven economic development and disparities in resource endowments (12). Second, the measurement of multidimensional relative poverty. Unlike absolute poverty, relative poverty was initially measured based on farm household income using relative income indicators. For example, the European Union uses 60% of median disposable income per capita as the threshold for relative poverty, while other studies have adopted varying benchmarks, such as 50% of average income (13), 60% of median income (14, 15), or 40% of disposable income (16). Although low income is a key factor contributing to poverty, it is not the only determinant of farmers' wellbeing (17), making it necessary to consider multiple dimensions.

Introduction: What “spatial poverty” means at a core level
- Core concept: Spatial poverty treats poverty as inherently a geographic phenomenon whose incidence, persistence, and severity vary across space, and whose meanings and thresholds are shaped by place, time, and institutions. <cite id="f215da46-0">In this view, poverty is not fixed in content but “changes significantly due to the influence of spatial dimensions,” so that “the content of the concept of poverty changes significantly due to the influence of spatial dimensions.”</cite> <cite id="f215da46-1">A spatial poverty theory maintains that “geographical location plays an important role in the formation and persistence of poverty” and has given rise to related ideas such as spatial poverty traps that can be empirically tested.</cite>
- Lineage and framing: <cite id="f215da46-1">Although environmental determinism has fallen out of favor, the “spatiality of poverty” has grown in relevance; spatial poverty theory inherits from determinism but emphasizes location’s role interacting with human decisions and institutions.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-0">Geographical approaches clarify the spatial distribution of poverty and emphasize how physical environment, infrastructure, distance to public resources, and demographic characteristics determine or interact with poverty in a place; possibilistic perspectives argue institutions and governance failures create spatial poverty traps.</cite>

Conceptual foundations and typologies
- Poverty as relative and multidimensional: <cite id="f215da46-2">There is no universally accepted, objective definition of poverty; institutions use different dimensions (income/expenditure, capabilities, social inclusion), reflecting multidimensional deprivation and context dependence.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-4">Poverty can be framed as income shortfalls, basic needs unmet, or capability deprivation, and is multidimensional, encompassing lack of access to health and education, social isolation, and powerlessness.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-2">The capability perspective defines poverty as deprivation of basic capabilities (nutrition, clothing, shelter, participation), not just low income.</cite>
- Absolute vs. relative poverty: <cite id="852e0cef-2">An absolute poverty line is the minimum income or consumption needed to meet basic needs (e.g., food, clothing, shelter), a concept rooted in work such as Ravallion (1992).</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-2">Relative poverty adjusts to average or median consumption levels; it classifies who is poor and tracks differences across regions by comparing households to local norms.</cite> <cite id="1c02d7de-1">Poverty is neither strictly absolute nor relative; definitions carry elements of both and are contested across the literature.</cite>
- Spatial poverty as a multidimensional/spatial deprivation concept: <cite id="1c02d7de-2">The World Bank’s early articulation of “multidimensional relative poverty” emphasized that human poverty encompasses lack of income and objective deprivations such as drinking water, roads, sanitation, and subjective perceptions of deprivation; later work expanded to spatial and ethnic-area analyses.</cite> <cite id="1c02d7de-0">Multidimensional relative poverty is a dynamic form in which health, education, and living standards fall significantly below the socially recognized average due to uneven development and endowment disparities, with EU-style thresholds like 60% of median income used for relative poverty measurement.</cite>

How “spatial poverty” is defined and operationalized in practice
- Income-based spatial thresholds and classification:
  - Global and national poverty lines: <cite id="852e0cef-0">The World Bank’s international poverty line is $1.90 per person per day (2011 PPPs), with lower- and upper-middle-income thresholds around $3.20 and $5.50 per day, used to classify households as poor based on income shortfalls.</cite>
  - Place-based relative thresholds: <cite id="852e0cef-1">Policy maps often classify “high-poverty tracts” using federal thresholds such as areas with >40% of the population below the official poverty line, or >20% for “extreme poverty” tracts; alternative lower thresholds (e.g., >30%) are used to capture concentrated poverty differently across metros.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-1">Relative, regional thresholds using 50% of local median income reveal a much greater extent and different geographic distribution of concentrated poverty than the federal line, underscoring how definition choice changes spatial patterns.</cite> <cite id="1c02d7de-0">EU practice uses 60% of median disposable income as a relative poverty threshold, with similar regional variants used elsewhere (50–40% of average or income) to reflect local standards.</cite>
  - Household targeting: <cite id="852e0cef-2">Once a line is set, incidence, depth, and severity are quantified using the Foster–Greer–Thorbecke (FGT) indices; headcount, gap, and squared gap measures formalize who is poor and how deprived they are.</cite>
- HDI-based spatial deprivation and multidimensional mapping:
  - Composite welfare benchmarks: <cite id="f215da46-1">Human Development Index (HDI) aggregates life expectancy, education, and income to capture welfare levels across countries and regions, providing a multidimensional reference for identifying spatial deprivation in rich and poor places.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-2">UNHDR defines poverty as “inadequacy of resources and deprivation of choices that would enable people to enjoy decent living conditions,” aligning with HDI-style multidimensional poverty concepts.</cite>
  - Operationalization in mapping: <cite id="852e0cef-0">Geographical theory is used to delineate spatial poverty by identifying areas where physical-environmental constraints, infrastructure deficits, distance to services, and governance failures co-locate to produce deprivation relative to regional standards.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-3">Administrative and empirical practice show that poverty is widely dispersed with localized concentrations; regional clustering and “spatial concentration effects” are often due to industry agglomeration and scale effects, motivating fine-scale (village-level) mapping for policy design.</cite>
- Spatial clustering and spillovers:
  - Concentration and outliers: <cite id="852e0cef-1">High-poverty “tracts” are commonly defined by thresholds like >40% under the line; studies vary thresholds (20–30–40%) to capture concentration versus isolated pockets.</cite>
  - Statistical diagnostics: <cite id="852e0cef-1">Relative definitions (e.g., 50% of median) reveal different spatial patterns and more widespread concentrated poverty than the federal line, highlighting sensitivity to the definition of “poverty” and its spatial distribution.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-4">Spatial clustering is assessed with local Moran’s I: counties with significantly positive neighbor correlations at standardized values >2 are “concentrations,” those with <−2 are “outliers,” enabling categorization of spatial outliers and clustered hotspots alongside poverty intensity.</cite>
- Country-level examples and measurement integration:
  - China’s rural line and MPI: <cite id="852e0cef-3">China’s rural poverty line tracked near the World Bank international threshold (2300–3535 yuan; ~$1.80–$2.76/day), enabling spatial targeting; multidimensional poverty indices (MPI) complement income lines, though indicator selection is challenging and single-dimensional measures remain common due to data simplicity.</cite>
  - Environmental–institutional determinants: <cite id="852e0cef-0">Geography-based poverty mapping integrates physical environment, infrastructure, distance to services, and governance quality to explain spatially varying poverty patterns and the risk of spatial poverty traps.</cite>

Mechanisms, evolution, and spatial spillovers
- Causal mechanisms: <cite id="852e0cef-0">Spatial poverty arises from interactions between physical conditions (vegetation, climate, soils, disasters, land use, resources) and human decisions, with infrastructure access, distance to public resources, and demographics shaping local deprivation; institutional and political failures produce spatial poverty traps.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-1">Geography of poverty explains the distribution, types, and evolutionary mechanisms of poverty, including interactions with the physical environment and anti-poverty interventions.</cite>
- Concentration, diffusion, and scale effects: <cite id="852e0cef-3">Globally, poverty areas tend to fragment spatially rather than expand in mass; at regional scales, poor areas cluster due to industry agglomeration, exhibiting spatial scale effects that matter for policy design.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-4">Local Moran’s I identifies spatial “concentrations” and “outliers,” revealing how poverty coevolves with wealth in contiguous counties and how isolated pockets reflect cross-border disparities.</cite>
- Measurement integration with welfare indicators: <cite id="852e0cef-2">FGT indices quantify incidence, depth, and severity of poverty once a threshold is chosen; inflation adjustment and adult-equivalence scaling are used to compare household status over time and space.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-1">The shift from one-dimensional lines to multidimensional indices reflects mainstreaming of poverty’s spatial and multidimensional qualities in theory and measurement.</cite>

Choice of definitions, scale, and critiques
- Relativity, arbitrariness, and context: <cite id="f215da46-4">There is no objectively correct poverty definition; different concepts and measures yield very different poverty rates and profiles, so clearer definitions suited to political, economic, and social context are essential.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-2">Definitions range from income shortfalls to basic needs to capability deprivation; each embeds different reference standards and may capture different aspects of deprivation.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-2">Absolute lines (minimum needs baskets) vs. relative lines (local averages/medians) imply different spatial classifications and target sets, with relative measures capturing inequality and place-based deprivation more directly.</cite>
- Threshold design and scale sensitivity: <cite id="852e0cef-1">Federal 40% thresholds and 50% of median income alternatives produce different spatial maps and concentration metrics, showing how threshold choice shapes conclusions about spatial poverty.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-1">Using a single monetary norm (e.g., 40% standard) can become “divorced from the realities of our affluent society,” motivating relative-region definitions that better capture meaningful differences across places.</cite>
- Data, indicators, and integration: <cite id="852e0cef-3">Multidimensional poverty measurement (MPI) integrates deprivations across health, education, and living standards, but indicator selection and data availability complicate implementation; single-dimensional lines remain common due to ease of use.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-3">Remote sensing (nighttime lights), internet/social media, and mobile phone transaction footprints enable proxy estimation of spatial poverty, complementing surveys and administrative data.</cite>
- Spatial methodology cautions: <cite id="852e0cef-0">Geographical poverty research clarifies local determinants and mechanisms, but thresholds and classifications hinge on context-specific standards; misaligning thresholds to place or time (e.g., fixed absolute baskets across regions) can distort spatial identification.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-2">Headcount and gap measures are sensitive to the poverty line; severity weights amplify inequality among the poor, so line choice and equivalence scales materially affect spatial poverty estimates.</cite>

Practical implications for defining and mapping spatial poverty
- Policy-relevant definitions:
  - Absolute-income poverty for targeting extreme deprivation (global lines; local baskets) to prioritize survival needs. <cite id="852e0cef-0">Global and national lines (e.g., $1.90/day) identify households below minimum needs and guide emergency and extreme poverty interventions.</cite>
  - Relative-income thresholds (e.g., 40–50% or 60% of median) to capture place-based deprivation and concentrated poverty for spatial planning. <cite id="852e0cef-1">Threats like >20–40% poverty delineate neighborhood-scale need; 50% of median income reveals broader concentrated poverty than official lines.</cite>
  - HDI/MPI-based spatial deprivation for multidimensional needs (health, education, infrastructure), recognizing capability loss and social exclusion. <cite id="1c02d7de-2">Multidimensional relative poverty integrates income and deprivations such as water, roads, sanitation, and subjective deprivation to reflect local living standards.</cite>
- Methods to implement:
  - Set a threshold; compute headcount and FGT indices; map spatial units using tract/county boundaries; test clustering with Moran’s I; classify concentrations/outliers; and create decile/ranking profiles combining intensity and spatial pattern. <cite id="852e0cef-2">Headcount, gap, and severity provide intensity metrics once the line is chosen.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-4">Local Moran’s I with standardized cutoffs (>2 or <−2 at p<0.05) identifies clustered hotspots and spatial outliers for spatial narratives.</cite>
- Governance and context: <cite id="852e0cef-0">Institutional and political factors can embed spatial poverty traps; mapping should integrate infrastructure access, distance to services, and governance quality to target structural bottlenecks alongside household income shortfalls.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-4">Because poverty is multidimensional, relying solely on income understates deprivation; integrating access, social inclusion, and power differentials yields a more actionable definition for place-based policy.</cite>

Summary answer to “What is spatial poverty and how is it defined?”
- Definition: Spatial poverty is the condition in which households or communities experience deprivation relative to locally recognized standards of living and access to goods and services, with incidence, intensity, and persistence varying across geographic space; poverty’s content is relational and contextual, shifting with place, time, and institutions. <cite id="f215da46-0">The concept of poverty changes significantly due to spatial dimensions.</cite> <cite id="f215da46-1">Geographical location plays an important role in the formation and persistence of poverty.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-0">Geographical theory explains spatial distribution and mechanisms, including interactions with physical environment and governance failures that produce spatial poverty traps.</cite>
- Core conceptual axes: It is neither purely absolute nor purely relative; it is multidimensional and dynamic across space and time, integrating income shortfalls with non-monetary deprivations and spillovers. <cite id="852e0cef-2">Absolute poverty lines fix minimum needs baskets; relative lines adjust to local averages/medians; both have roles but are context-dependent.</cite> <cite id="852e0cef-3">Spatial poverty often combines widespread dispersion with localized concentrations shaped by regional industry and scale effects.</cite>
- Operational definitions used:

Snippet: At the fundamental level is the question of who qualifies as the poor or what is poverty. This conceptual question has plagued development practices and policymakers for several decades. The task of defining poverty assumed greater relevance in the 1960s in the aftermath of the attainment of political independence by many former colonies (Lee & Braithwaite, 2022). Suffice it to state that defining poverty or even the approach to doing this, is a strongly contested issue and the different positions are not always necessarily complementary. One of the well-known theorizations in this endeavour is the capability approach by Sen (1982Sen ( , 2000) ) who posits that the specification of a certain consumption norm or of a poverty line does only a part of the job. This notwithstanding, the World Bank still annually publishes its report based on a hypothetical dollar per person per day metriccurrently, 1.9 USD per person per day -as the so-called poverty line while the United Nations produces its annual reports on the human development index -a composite of life expectancy, education and standard of living -to measure welfare levels in individual countries. There has been a clear move towards indices as the multidimensional nature of poverty has become more mainstream (Alkire & Foster, 2011). 

A key development in this theoretical evolution has been the discovery of the spatial qualities of poverty and deprivation. The theory of spatial poverty can be traced back to the theory of environmental determinism -the idea that the physical environment predisposes regions and countries to particular development trajectories. While environmental determinism has largely been rejected in favour of environmental possibilism, the spatiality of poverty continues to grow in relevance (Bird et al., 2010;Burke & Jayne, 2008;Elwood et al., 2016). Like its antecedent, the spatial poverty theory holds that geographical location plays an important role in the formation and persistence of poverty (Zhou & Liu, 2022). It has, in turn, spawned other concepts such as spatial poverty traps which are empirically verifiable.

Snippet: An accurate definition of poverty is crucial to help organizations and governments understand which citizens and communities are most in need. Many institutions and scholars have attempted to define poverty, but a concise and universally accepted definition of poverty has never been emerged. There is some arbitrariness in any definition of poverty if keeping an eye on different dimensions and the tools used to measure poverty. There are number of factors that cause poverty because of which there exist number of definitions of poverty. Poverty may include social, economic, and political elements. Encyclopedia Encarta defines poverty as "the condition of having insufficient resources or income". According to the United Nations Human Development Report (UNHDR, 1998), poverty is defined as "a complex phenomenon that generally refers to inadequacy of resources and deprivation of choices that would enable people to enjoy decent living condition.'' A renowned Indian economist, Amartya Sen, (Sen.A, 1999) has argued that poverty should be seen as the deprivation of basic capabilities, where that deprivation limits the freedom of a person to pursue their goals in life. In the broadest sense, it means survival but also contribution and participation to social daily activities. For Sen 'capability deprivation' is a better measure of poverty than lowness of income. From the various definitions given above, it is clear that the concept of poverty is a complex phenomenon influenced by large number of factors. The study and interpretation of poverty is not an easy task as there are many ways of measuring poverty as there are ways of defining it. The measurement and definition of poverty depend on how it is viewed, how one like to study and interpret. Poverty thus has been a complex concept, having a range of meaning.

Title: Poverty: A Literature Review of the Concept, Measurements, Causes and the Way Forward
Snippet: In spite of the fact that there is some lucidity within the field of poverty with respect to the concept, measurements, causes, and the way forward, those exterior to the field are confronted with an apparently complex poverty literature, overlapping terminology, and several published measures. Therefore, the objective of this review was to give an overview of concepts, measurements, causes and the way forward on poverty. A systematic literature review was performed by searching websites, and electronic databases from January 2000 to September 2020, and the selected articles were then analyzed thematically. Twenty research articles, and 23 website articles were incorporated in the analysis. In the current paper authors try to develop a guidance to the academicians and policy makers who are looking to use poverty in their work. Further, it gives an outline of the various conceptualizations of poverty, and afterward give a set of recommendations for researchers, and practitioners with respect to the most appropriate measures of poverty for a scope of various purposes, and policy implications for the way forward the poverty.

Snippet: Reducing poverty and inequality is a cornerstone of development policy of any nation [1]. Poverty definitions and measurements have important ramifications for targeting its reduction strategies [2]. While there is a widespread agreement on the desirability of poverty reduction, defining poverty is more controversial. There is no objectively correct definition of poverty, and most commentators accept that any definition must be understood in relation to a specific political, economic and social context [3]. Empirical evidence suggest that poverty rates vary a lot when different concepts and measures are used, thus clearer definitions and measures are essential for poverty-centred development policies [2]. Poverty can be conceptualised and measured in different ways. The conventional economic approach focuses on the quantifiable poverty lines based solely on consumption and expenditure patterns. While the poverty line is an important measure of poverty in a country over time, poverty goes beyond income level: it includes lack of access to health and education, respect, isolation from the community, and a feeling of powerlessness and hopelessness. Poverty is actually multi-dimensional, and many of its dimensions are often hidden. People whose main source of income is their farm, are five-times more likely to be poor than their counterparts who receive a wage from the public or private sector [4]. Handley et al. [5] posited that poverty is not an easy concept to define, as a result a range of definitions exist, influenced by different disciplinary approaches and ideologies. Madulu [6] reported that a poor person is a one whose standard of living falls below the minimum acceptable level (poverty line), and can be absolute or relative. Poverty is a multidimensional phenomenon, and can be defined using three different concepts: income, basic needs, and capability. Of these, the most commonly used concept is income, where a person is poor if her/ his income is below a certain amount. The basic need concept considers material requirements for a minimally fulfilling life. These are normally understood to include factors such as basic health care and education. The capability perspective concentrates on factors such as adequate nutrition, clothing and shelter, but also considers social aspects such as partaking in the life of the community [3,5]. 

There are many definitions, as well as intense debate, about the poverty situation.

Snippet: the geographical theory of poverty clarifies the spatial distribution of poverty (Bradshaw, 2006;chimhowu, 2009;tian et al., 2018). it explains, according to Zhou and liu (2022), the spatial distribution, spatial types, and evolutionary mechanisms of poverty, as well as its interactions with the physical environment and anti-poverty initiatives, based on deterministic and possibilistic approaches. in the views of okwi et al. Title: The common prosperity effect of rural households' financial participation: a perspective based on multidimensional relative poverty
Snippet: Current research on multidimensional relative poverty focuses on three key areas. First, the conceptual evolution of multidimensional relative poverty. Poverty studies have gradually shifted from absolute and relative poverty to multidimensional and multidimensional relative poverty. Initially, absolute poverty was defined as a state where a household's total income could not cover the basic necessities required by all its members to maintain normal bodily functions (6). With a deeper understanding of poverty, scholars argued that it also includes relative exclusion and deprivation, leading to the development of the relative poverty theory (7). However, relative poverty has its limitations (8), necessitating consideration of various factors that affect the long-term wellbeing of impoverished individuals, such as health, education, and quality of life (9). Consequently, some scholars argue for the establishment of a multidimensional poverty measurement system to address the comprehensive development needs of the poor (10). While multidimensional relative poverty is distinct from multidimensional poverty, the concept of relative poverty emphasizes differences among individuals. Its measurement dimensions and indicators cannot be directly equated with those of multidimensional poverty. Furthermore, existing research on multidimensional relative poverty often adopts the measurement dimensions of multidimensional poverty without adequately addressing the distinctions in measurement elements (11). Multidimensional relative poverty is a dynamic form of poverty characterized by a state of living in which a family's health, education, and standard of living are significantly below the socially recognized average due to factors such as uneven economic development and disparities in resource endowments (12). Second, the measurement of multidimensional relative poverty. Unlike absolute poverty, relative poverty was initially measured based on farm household income using relative income indicators. For example, the European Union uses 60% of median disposable income per capita as the threshold for relative poverty, while other studies have adopted varying benchmarks, such as 50% of average income (13), 60% of median income (14, 15), or 40% of disposable income (16). Although low income is a key factor contributing to poverty, it is not the only determinant of farmers' wellbeing (17), making it necessary to consider multiple dimensions.

Title: Dynamics of Poverty in Developing Countries: Review of Poverty Reduction Approaches
Snippet: Although Alcock (1993) claims that absolute poverty is objective and represents a scientific notion, it has been argued that definitions of absolute poverty contain some elements of relativity (Noble et al., 2004). The 'relative' concept of poverty connotes a standard of living in relation to the position of other people in the income/expenditure distribution, and defines poverty basically as a phenomenon of inequality (Bellu, 2005). snippet.text: Current research on multidimensional relative poverty focuses on three key areas. First, the conceptual evolution of multidimensional relative poverty. Poverty studies have gradually shifted from absolute and relative poverty to multidimensional and multidimensional relative poverty. Initially, absolute poverty was defined as a state where a household's total income could not cover the basic necessities required by all its members to maintain normal bodily functions (6). With a deeper understanding of poverty, scholars argued that it also includes relative exclusion and deprivation, leading to the development of the relative poverty theory (7). However, relative poverty has its limitations (8), necessitating consideration of various factors that affect the long-term wellbeing of impoverished individuals, such as health, education, and quality of life (9). Consequently, some scholars argue for the establishment of a multidimensional poverty measurement system to address the comprehensive development needs of the poor (10). While multidimensional relative poverty is distinct from multidimensional poverty, the concept of relative poverty emphasizes differences among individuals. Its measurement dimensions and indicators cannot be directly equated with those of multidimensional poverty. Furthermore, existing research on multidimensional relative poverty often adopts the measurement dimensions of multidimensional poverty without adequately addressing the distinctions in measurement elements (11). Multidimensional relative poverty is a dynamic form of poverty characterized by a state of living in which a family's health, education, and standard of living are significantly below the socially recognized average due to factors such as uneven economic development and disparities in resource endowments (12). Second, the measurement of multidimensional relative poverty. Unlike absolute poverty, relative poverty was initially measured based on farm household income using relative income indicators. For example, the European Union uses 60% of median disposable income per capita as the threshold for relative poverty, while other studies have adopted varying benchmarks, such as 50% of average income (13), 60% of median income (14, 15), or 40% of disposable income (16). Although low income is a key factor contributing to poverty, it is not the only determinant of farmers' wellbeing (17), making it necessary to consider multiple dimensions.

Summary
Across economics, geography, and sociology, poverty is not just an individual income state but a place-bound condition in which people are relationally and materially excluded from the opportunities and capabilities that others in their society take for granted. A core unified definition therefore treats spatial poverty as the insecure or inadequate access that people in a given place have to valued goods, services, and social prospects, relative to social norms and expectations, where “spatial” captures how distance, local assets, and place-based institutions shape who is included or excluded. <cite id="c4ed6cdb-4">Beyond economic figures, poverty relates to the ability to access common goods such as education and health, and multidimensional approaches like the Alkire–Foster method capture this access orientation</cite> <cite id="c4ed6cdb-3">Poverty encompasses lack of opportunities, empowerment, security, and access to social services, and is spatially heterogeneous with clustering shaped by infrastructure and services</cite> <cite id="bfae8f80-1">Economic, geographic, and sociological research all document substantial geographic variation in deprivation and disadvantage, motivating area-based and multidimensional measures</cite>.

Why a unified definition is needed
Economics has long emphasized income shortfalls and their geographic patterning; geography highlights spatial distributions, gradients, and access to opportunities; sociology foregrounds embeddedness, social processes, and spatial justice. <cite id="bfae8f80-1">Across disciplines, studies at county, tract, and neighborhood scales show poverty varies markedly across geographic contexts, with persistent geographic disparities over time and evolving with demographics and conditions</cite> <cite id="c4ed6cdb-1">Geography integrates spatial analysis methods—autocorrelation, interaction, and accessibility—to explain localized poverty and its diffusion processes</cite> <cite id="07b9bd93-0">Spatial justice defines equity as an equitable distribution of resources and opportunities and fairness in the relations of power shaping social space, distinguishing spatial from social justice but linking both to justice</cite>. Bridging these perspectives requires a definition that treats material deprivation and multidimensional deprivations as manifestations of place-mediated access failures. <cite id="c4ed6cdb-3">Poverty is a state of lacking goods and services needed for a decent standard of living, including infrastructure, services, and security</cite> <cite id="c4ed6cdb-0">Local geographic capital—natural, social, and economic assets—shapes regional poverty, with deficits producing spatial poverty traps</cite>.

A core unified definition
Spatial poverty is the condition in which people or groups in a given place have insecure or inadequate access, relative to social expectations, to valued goods and opportunities—economic, social, and civic—because access is constrained by place: local assets, infrastructure, institutions, and spatial structure, as well as distance and territorial organization. <cite id="c4ed6cdb-4">This definition centers access to common goods and capabilities beyond income, aligning with multidimensional poverty frameworks</cite> <cite id="bfae8f80-1">Geographic disparities in deprivation motivate place-based measurement of disadvantage</cite> <cite id="07b9bd93-0">Spatial justice emphasizes fair distribution of resources and opportunities and the role of spatial relations of power</cite>. Put differently, spatial poverty captures the intersection of material deprivation with spatial opportunity gaps and place-based exclusion, where the same bundle of capabilities is harder to achieve for residents of poorly connected or under-resourced places. <cite id="c4ed6cdb-3">The poor tend to cluster in places with inadequate infrastructure and services, making access-based deprivations persistent</cite> <cite id="bfae8f80-2">Urban poverty features inadequate income, assets, shelter, public infrastructure, and basic services, often culminating in socio-spatial fragmentation and segregation</cite>.

How the definition reconciles the three research traditions
Economics. Economic work on the geography of poverty emphasizes how place-based variation in income and composite deprivation reflects local “geographic capital” and opportunity access. <cite id="bfae8f80-1">County-, tract-, and neighborhood-level indicators show substantial and persistent geographic variation in multidimensional deprivation</cite> <cite id="bfae8f80-1">Area-based indices (e.g., ADI, NDI) and geographically disaggregated multidimensional measures identify heterogeneous disadvantage across space</cite> <cite id="c4ed6cdb-4">Geographic capital—human, social, financial, physical, natural, and livelihood capital—forms the regional foundation that enables development; deficits in capital create spatial poverty and traps</cite>. Mechanistically, the unified definition absorbs these findings by viewing income insufficiency as one channel through which limited place-based assets and services restrict utility-maximizing access to goods and opportunities.

Geography. Geographic traditions bring spatial processes, access, and scale to the center. <cite id="c4ed6cdb-1">Geography studies distances, contiguity, accessibility, and spatial diffusion to explain localized poverty, using autocorrelation and interaction models</cite> <cite id="bfae8f80-2">Urban poverty exhibits spatial agglomeration, inadequate assets and infrastructure, and socio-spatial fragmentation, with “island effects” where poverty concentrates in areas with poor geographic conditions</cite> <cite id="bfae8f80-3">Spatial features of regional poverty vary by scale, and concepts like spatial poverty traps, environmental determinism, and “island effect” tie local opportunity deficits to outcomes</cite>. The unified definition integrates these by treating spatial poverty as the distribution of access capacities across geography, measured by gradients, clustering, and spatial dependence in multidimensional deprivations.

Sociology. Sociological and critical geographies emphasize embeddedness, social reproduction, and spatial justice. <cite id="07b9bd93-0">Spatial justice calls for equitable distribution of resources and fairness in the relations of power that shape social space</cite> <cite id="07b9bd93-2">Neighborhood effects research reveals reinforcement and consequences of disadvantage, while critiques of “deconcentration” and social mixing show how structural factors like discrimination, limited opportunities, and resource access reproduce segregation</cite> <cite id="07b9bd93-1">Social geography centers justice as addressing unfair outcomes from social processes and institutional decisions, making the social fabric and policy context central to poverty and welfare</cite>. The unified definition captures these mechanisms by framing spatial poverty as relational exclusion embedded in local institutions and networks, where norms, stigma, and territorial control interact with material constraints to limit capabilities.

Mechanisms and gradients captured by the definition
- Asset and opportunity deficits: <cite id="c4ed6cdb-0">Local geographic capital deficits (natural, social, economic) generate spatial poverty traps</cite> <cite id="c4ed6cdb-3">Geographic variation in infrastructure and services shapes clustering and persistence</cite>.

- Cumulative place effects on wellbeing: <cite id="07b9bd93-3">Longitudinal spatial evidence shows childhood residence in disadvantaged neighborhoods harms later mental health, and local employment conditions are associated with onset of long-term illness; place-based resources can be equigenic, reducing inequities</cite>.
- Scale dependence: <cite id="bfae8f80-3">Regional poverty’s multiscale features differ across localities, guiding differentiated policy responses</cite>.

Conceptually, spatial poverty can be measured at multiple levels, aligning metrics to the definition’s access orientation and spatial scope.
- Individual-level capabilities: <cite id="c4ed6cdb-3">Multidimensional indicators encompass lack of opportunities, empowerment, security, and access to social services</cite> <cite id="c4ed6cdb-4">Alkire–Foster multidimensional poverty captures overlapping deprivations and is sensitive to relative issues across countries</cite>.
- Area-level deprivation and access gradients: <cite id="bfae8f80-1">Geographically disaggregated multidimensional indices and area deprivation indices reveal hotspots and persistent spatial heterogeneity</cite> <cite id="bfae8f80-2">Urban indicators highlight inadequate infrastructure and services as core manifestations of spatial poverty</cite>.
- Spatial process diagnostics: <cite id="c4ed6cdb-1">Spatial autocorrelation, interaction, and diffusion models diagnose clustering, spatial spillovers, and center–periphery dynamics</cite> <cite id="bfae8f80-2">Island effects and agglomeration patterns identify places with limited natural endowments, fragile ecosystems, and poor conditions</cite>.
- Justice and policy coherence: <cite id="07b9bd93-0">Spatial justice frameworks assess equity in resource and opportunity distribution and fairness in spatial power relations, informing place-based policy design</cite>.

Implications and open issues
- Integrating income and access: <cite id="c4ed6cdb-4">Income-based and multidimensional measures capture different facets; area-based indices complement individual measures by locating capability deficits in place</cite> <cite id="bfae8f80-1">Geographically disaggregated measures help target overlapping deprivations</cite>.
- Place-based vs people-based: <cite id="bfae8f80-2">Poverty can be regional or individual, rural or urban, with binaries interrelated; micro-level heterogeneity complicates measurement and requires fine-scale spatial identification</cite>.
- Spurious “neighborhood effects” vs structural constraints: <cite id="07b9bd93-2">Causal interpretation hinges on distinguishing symptom-from-cause; neighborhood effects can reflect place-based structural reproduction rather than purely intra-household dynamics</cite>.
- Causal inference and multi-level mechanisms: <cite id="c4ed6cdb-2">Integrating causal methods (e.g., EO–ML) with spatial analysis can test mechanisms linking place characteristics to deprivation outcomes across scales</cite>.
- Scale and mobility: <cite id="bfae8f80-3">Spatial features vary by scale, requiring multi-level diagnostics for policy coherence</cite> <cite id="07b9bd93-3">Long-run residence in disadvantaged places carries lasting wellbeing penalties, suggesting persistent spatial poverty dynamics</cite>.

Conclusion
A unified, cross-disciplinary definition of spatial poverty treats it as the place-mediated condition of insecure or inadequate access to valued opportunities and capabilities relative to social expectations, produced by local assets, infrastructure, institutions, and spatial structures, and manifested as geographic concentration, gradients, and multidimensional deprivations. <cite id="bfae8f80-1">Economic analyses document geographic variation and area-based deprivation</cite> <cite id="c4ed6cdb-0">Geographic capital deficits and spatial poverty traps</cite> <cite id="c4ed6cdb-3">Access to services and infrastructure</cite> <cite id="07b9bd93-0">Spatial justice and equitable distribution of resources and opportunities</cite> <cite id="07b9bd93-2">Segregation logics and territorial reproduction of disadvantage</cite> <cite id="07b9bd93-3">Cumulative effects of place on health and wellbeing</cite> collectively converge on this definition, offering a bridge across geographic, economic, and sociological traditions. <cite id="c4ed6cdb-1">Geography’s spatial methods and multidisciplinary measurement</cite> provide the tools to operationalize and evaluate it across scales and contexts.

Snippet: Interest in the geographic distribution of poverty has a long history within economics, geography, sociology, and public policy. These studies established the importance of considering geographic context when evaluating socioeconomic disadvantage and laid the conceptual and empirical foundation for subsequent multidimensional analyses of geographic deprivation. 

More recently, researchers have increasingly applied multidimensional approaches to investigate the geographic distribution of deprivation. Dhongde and Haveman documented considerable differences in multidimensional deprivation across U.S. regions and states, providing early evidence that the incidence and composition of deprivation vary geographically and are not fully reflected by conventional income-poverty measures [6]. Expanding upon this work, Dhongde and Haveman examined spatial and temporal trends in multidimensional poverty using ACS data, demonstrating that geographic disparities persist over time while also evolving in response to changing demographic, economic, and social conditions [9]. 

The U.S. Census Bureau has likewise emphasized the geographic application of multidimensional deprivation measures. Glassman introduced the Census Bureau's MDI [10], while subsequent work extended its geographic application through state-and countylevel estimation using publicly available ACS data [15,16]. These studies demonstrate the practical value of geographically disaggregated multidimensional measures for identifying areas experiencing multiple, overlapping forms of disadvantage. 

A related literature has developed area-based measures of socioeconomic disadvantage, including the Area Deprivation Index (ADI), the Neighborhood Deprivation Index (NDI), and related composite indicators [17][18][19][20]. Although these indices differ conceptually from Alkire-Foster multidimensional poverty measures-typically characterizing the socioeconomic conditions of geographic areas rather than identifying multidimensionally deprived individuals-they likewise demonstrate marked geographic heterogeneity across states, counties, metropolitan areas, neighborhoods, and other geographic units. These studies reinforce the importance of incorporating geographic context into analyses of deprivation and socioeconomic disadvantage. 

Although these studies share a common objective of characterizing geographic disadvantages, they differ in both their methodological approaches and geographic scope.

Title: Spatial justice on the horizon? A combined Theory of Change scenario tool to assess place-based interventions
Snippet: Spatial justice has been defined as 'an equitable spatial distribution of resources and opportunities, and fairness in the relations of power that shape and transform the social space' (Madanipour et al. 2020, 75). Spatial justice focuses primarily on the implication for justice of spatiality, and the concept draws upon but is distinguished from social justice, which instead focuses on the distribution of resources across social groups. 

In terms of how spatial justice is understood and responded to in EU policy, it is not systematically addressed by the European Social Model. This model pursues social justice instead, though there is no official definition of this concept, but rather a 'conceptual abstraction' incorporating the EU's attempt to strike a balance between individuals, the state and the market (Madanipour et al. 2020, 21). The EU Cohesion Policy seems more closely related to spatial justice given its focus on wellbeing across space. The Barca Report (2009) recognised that 'place-based development strategies' are more effective in promoting the catch-up of lagging areas than neo-liberal approaches, which ignore spatial specificities and can thus be argued to be spatially-blind. Placebased policy is defined in the Report as a 'long-term strategy aimed at tackling persistent underutilisation of potential and reducing persistent social exclusion in specific places through external interventions and multilevel governance' (Barca 2009: viii). The EU Community-led Local Development programme (previously LEADER) exemplifies how place-based approaches have been applied in practice. But despite place-based development becoming more prominent in the Cohesion Policy rhetoric, cohesion programmes are often shaped by strategic choices of national and regional authorities rather than being bottom-up (Madanipour et al. 2020). 

The EU covers a large diversity of places, and place-based interventions addressing spatial justice therein. However, a systematic approach to assess the internal and external 'coherence' of such interventions, including their response to changing contextual conditions in increasingly uncertain local, national and international situations, is lacking. Such an approach would help enhance the coherence of policy design and evaluation by showing what it is and is not working well, thus delivering sustainable outputs and, ultimately, outcomes (Nilsson and Weitz 2019).

Title: Social geography III: Committing to social justice
Snippet: In this final report about contemporary social geography, I turn to the topic of social justice, a key underpinning principle for much work in the sub-discipline. Social justice is about addressing the unfair outcomes that result from both social processes and institutional decisionmaking. It is not just about individual fairness but also about the distribution of society's benefits and burdens (Smith, 2000a(Smith, , 2000b)); it is socio-political (Thompson, 2016;Olson, 2018) and raises wider moral questions. Social justice intersects and overlaps with debates and issues relating to equality and diversity and so is a key dimension of anti-discriminatory practice (Thompson, 2016); as Smith (2000a) noted, a just society is always underpinned by equality. Seeking spatial justice is, as Soja (2010: 2) put it, 'a struggle over geography'. 

Social geographers have particular strengths in exploring lived experiences of those suffering due to social inequalities, including offering critiques of problematic government policies or welfare regimes; moreover, social geographers are skilled at doing this work in a whole host of engaging, creative and activist ways. However, a lot less attention is paid in social geography to what social justice looks like and feels like, and what policies might be put in place to make social justice a reality. Oswin (2018: 614) notes that 'these are frustrating and downright frightening times and we simply must think deeply about the ways in which multiple forms of domination work in concert to maintain and intensify an inequitable and violent status quo'. One of the main arguments in this review is that there is a tendency to sidestep social justice in social geography rather than engaging with it directly. Yet, Oswin (2018) urges that we should keep telling it like it is and, in concert with this call, I argue that social geography is committed to social justice and so should be explicitly political in advocating for it. 

I appraise debates about social justice before moving on to review recent work that engages directly with social justice or with debates about exclusion, marginalisation and inequality. I pay specific attention to three areas: poverty and welfare, gender and sexuality, and race and ethnicity.

Title: Health geographies II: Resilience, health and place
Snippet: Health geographers are developing dynamic conceptualizations to understand and measure the cumulative and causal impact of place for individual health over time (Pearce, 2018;Kwan, 2018;Dearden et al., 2019). For example, Lucy Prior et al. (2019) propose 'exposomic' health geographies to engage with biodata resources across large-scale social surveys. These would provide more-than-individual social perspectives, informed by better understanding of place. Longitudinal spatial work establishes the cumulative impact of place over the entire life course from childhood to old age, showing how residing in socially-disadvantaged neighbourhoods in childhood was detrimental to mental health outcomes at age 70 (Pearce et al., 2018). Sarah Curtis and colleagues' (2019) work with UK longitudinal spatial data shows how, even controlling for other determinants of health (ethnicity, age, home ownership, employment), changes in local employment conditions over time have significant associations with onset of new longterm illness. In other research, they demonstrate how wellbeing improved less overall for those living in more disadvantaged areas over 5 years (Curtis et al., 2020). 

Combinations of salutogenic or pathogenic attributes and resources of places (like alcohol-outlet or gambling venue density, access to services, housing quality and type or access to public transport or green-space) contribute to resilience by reinforcing or preventing positive health and social outcomes including equity. Hannah Badland and Jamie Pearce (2019) use an environmental justice lens to show how urban resources are 'equigenic' or able to disrupt the usual relationship between economic disadvantage and poor health outcomes and reduce inequities. For example, high-quality school environments have disproportionately positive effects for socio-economically disadvantaged children. There is growing evidence for the value of placebased resources to support individual and collective resilience; this also provides an evidence-base supporting decisions about the most appropriate spatial scale at which to introduce interventions. For example, qualitative research on fuel poverty in Australia (Waitt and Harada, 2019) and Hong Kong (Fong and O'Sullivan, 2021) offers insights into the material and emotional dimensions of tenants' efforts to manage energy bills at home through thrifty consumption practices around heating, cooling or using appliances or hot water.
